content_items.title: A community-curated controlled vocabulary for fossil collections using dwc:materialEntityType

programme.title: Developing a community-curated controlled vocabulary for fossil collections using the term dwc:materialEntityType
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract:
Data about fossil specimens are not always easy to distinguish from that related to modern material, especially when aggregated in broadly scoped platforms such as the Global Biodiversity Information Facility. While fossil specimens have traditionally relied on the dwc:basisOfRecord term to distinguish themselves, this needs to be reconsidered given the recent ratification of a conceptual model for Darwin Core, and the associated Darwin Core Data Package. With these, the terms dwc:materialEntityCategory and dwc:materialEntityType are expected to functionally replace dwc:basisOfRecord in the evolution of publishing data using the Darwin Core standard. The term dwc:materialEntityCategory aims to define a broad category identifying the nature of a dwc:MaterialEntity with a tightly controlled vocabulary including the value "fossil" or "fossilized." dwc:materialEntityType is a narrower concept for which we expect controlled vocabularies to be more discipline-specific.

We have been coordinating members of the paleontological research and collections communities to build consensus around a controlled vocabulary that fossil collections can use with dwc:materialEntityType. This vocabulary would streamline research requests and facilitate collections management workflows by enabling users to gain a better understanding of the physical material represented by the digital record. For example, looking at two current records of fossil insects without images, it would not be obvious if one was preserved in amber and another was a compression fossil on a slab. We propose an initial controlled vocabulary focused on a relatively small set of concepts, potentially to be expanded to sub-concepts in a future proposal. Here we present the process and our preliminary proposed vocabulary.

speakers.name: Holly Little
speakers.affiliation: Department of Paleobiology, Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History

actual.identification_notes: Speaker introduced by the host and self-identified; co-author Talia (Karim) was in the room and Erica Krimmel online.

content_items.summary: Holly Little explained why the new Darwin Core terms materialEntityCategory and materialEntityType (from the Darwin Core Data Package work) give paleontology collections a chance to go beyond basisOfRecord = FossilSpecimen. Using examples (insects in amber versus compression fossils, bivalves in matrix, forams as bulk samples, picks, slides or macrofossils, trilobite mass-mortality slabs) she showed that early values such as macrofossil/mesofossil/microfossil are too coarse for search, research and imaging planning. The group proposes a first-level controlled vocabulary drawn from terms collections already use, with an informal second level, and is seeking community feedback via a QR-linked document before formal proposal to Darwin Core.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A granular, community-derived vocabulary for dwc:materialEntityType would let users filter fossil records by what the material actually is, which basisOfRecord cannot do.
content_items.why_it_matters: Fossil records in aggregators like GBIF are hard to filter by the kind of physical material; a shared vocabulary improves discoverability for researchers and planning for collections staff (e.g. imaging workflows).
key_points: basisOfRecord = FossilSpecimen only separates fossils from other record types; it cannot distinguish e.g. an insect in amber from a compression fossil.

materialEntityCategory would carry 'fossil'/'fossilized', while materialEntityType can be more specific; early proposed values (macro-, meso-, micro-, oversized fossil) were judged not granular enough.
Feedback was gathered from the Paleo Data Working Group, researchers, a session at the Smithsonian NMNH, the TDWG Earth Sciences and Paleobiology Interest Group and a US collections workshop.
The vocabulary prioritises terms the paleo community already uses; some perceived overlap between terms is intentional.
Proposal is hierarchical: a formal first level plus an informal nested second level for institutions wanting more detail.
It covers paleontology only; geology material types are handled by a separate vocabulary Ben Norton is developing.
Other terms (dwc:preparations, counts, taxonomy, Latimer Core terms) help but are uncontrolled, not indexed or not in Darwin Core; a morphology term does not yet exist.

content_items.title: Extending Specify 7 for geological collections (GeoSpecify)

programme.title: Extending Specify 7 for Geological Collections
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract:
For 25 years, Specify has provided biological research museums and genetic repositories with software and technical services for curating, integrating, and publishing collections information. With funding from the Swiss Academy of Sciences (SwissCollNet initiative) and in collaboration with four Swiss natural history museums (Basel, Bern, Lausanne, Geneva), the Specify Collections Consortium (SCC) extended Specify to support geological collections.

Geocollections database requirements are similar in many ways to those of biological collections, however their unique properties and cataloging protocols challenged us to extend Specify concepts and capabilities. In addition to adding new tables, such as Absolute and Relative Age, and a new tree, Tectonic Unit, Specify added support for new protocols, most notably, Collection Object Groups (COGs), Components, and Collection Object Types (COTs).

In this presentation, SCC staff will discuss and demonstrate the new tables, tree, and features added to the Specify schema in order to support Geology Collections and their unique needs. These new features were designed to also support functionality required by Natural History Collections, the backbone of our membership.

The SCC is an open-source, collections community collaborative governed, funded, and sustained by its member institutions. Our software and technical support priorities address member data and system infrastructure needs. With Specify’s extension into the earth sciences, natural history museums will now be able to curate, integrate, and publish data from a robustly engineered single platform for both biological and geological collections.

speakers.name: Theresa Miller
speakers.affiliation: Specify Collections Consortium

actual.identification_notes: Name transcribed as 'Teresa Miller'.

content_items.summary: Theresa Miller presented GeoSpecify, the SwissCollNet-funded collaboration (Natural History Museum Bern, Specify Collections Consortium, Ben Norton) that extended the existing Specify 7 data model for geology rather than building a separate system. After requirements gathering with Swiss museums and an advisory committee, Specify gained an improved chronostratigraphy tree with start/end ages and biostratigraphy flags, a tectonic unit tree, an extended Geologic Context table, one-to-many relative and absolute age tables, and an 'extended age query' that searches all age fields by name or numeric range with strict or non-strict matching. Collection object types, discipline default forms, collection object groups (discrete, consolidated, drill core) and components allow mixed rock, mineral and fossil collections in one system, with Darwin Core Archive export planned to include the mineralogy extension.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: GeoSpecify brings geology into the same Specify data model as biological collections, with purpose-built age, stratigraphy and composite-object features.
content_items.why_it_matters: Institutions with mixed biological, paleontological and geological holdings can manage them in one standards-aligned system and publish geology data via Darwin Core.
key_points: Project led by Beda Hofmann (NHM Bern), James Beach (Specify) and Ben Norton, funded via the Swiss Academy of Sciences' SwissCollNet; phase 1 (from 2023) built a conceptual model and classification, phase 2 defined requirements and implementation.
Requirements came from four Swiss collections (Bern, Basel, Geneva, Lausanne), a GeoSpecify advisory committee and an on-site requirements trip; needs included warnings for heavy or toxic specimens.
Chronostratigraphy tree shows start/end dates, links to the International Chronostratigraphic Chart, stays ordered by age and can flag biostratigraphy nodes.
Lithostratigraphy and a new Tectonic Unit tree are populated locally because terms vary by region.
Geologic Context links to all stratigraphic trees and supports start and end chronostratigraphic periods; relative and absolute ages are one-to-many (e.g. deposition and metamorphism ages).
Extended age query searches geologic context, relative and absolute ages together, converting period names to numeric ranges and supporting strict/non-strict range matching.

Collection Object Types let one collection hold minerals, rocks and fossils with different trees, forms and numbering; Collection Object Groups (discrete, consolidated, drill core) and components capture composite specimens.
Data can be exported as Darwin Core Archive/RSS; the mineralogy extension will be an export option once accepted by GBIF.

content_items.title: Improving access to Earth science collections data via GeoCASe and the European Open Science Cloud (GeoDARA)

programme.title: Improving Access to Earth Science Collections Data via GeoCASe and the European Open Science Cloud
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract: Earth Science collections curated by natural history museums and research institutions contain critical records documenting past climates, environmental change, natural hazards, biodiversity dynamics, and geological processes across deep time. Despite their considerable scientific and societal value, these data have often remained fragmented, inconsistently described, and difficult to integrate with other Earth observation datasets. The CETAF Earth Science Group (ESG) is working to improve the discoverability, interoperability, and reuse of Earth Science collections data across Europe. ESG is leading the further development of GeoCASe (https://geocase.eu), a data network, aggregation service, and web portal for geoscientific collections data. The recently launched EOSC-Gravity project “Geodera” aims to integrate geological specimen-and sample-level data within the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC) through their Data Terra thematic node. Geodera will use representative case studies from different branches of geology to analyse and identify researchers’ data service needs, and to evaluate the usefulness of collections-based records for scientific applications and cross-domain research. Particular attention will be given to metadata harmonisation with external research platforms and datasets, including Earth observation data services within EOSC and Data Terra. This work includes assessing existing TDWG community standards, such as ABCD and Darwin Core, together with their geoscience extensions, as well as emerging concepts such as digital specimens. The project will identify gaps in current metadata schemas, provide training and practical guidelines to improve data quality, expand the GeoCASe consortium, and strengthen interoperability across the Earth Sciences domain.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded virtual talk by Laura Tilley; co-author Patricia Mergen was present in the room to take questions. Part of the audio (about 00:35:36-00:36:09) was lost while sound problems were fixed, and the recording restarted briefly at the end (00:45:09).

content_items.summary: Laura Tilley described GeoDARA, a six-month (May-November) EOSC Gravity small project by the CETAF Earth Science Group and partners exploring how earth science collection data can be made more FAIR through GeoCASe and connected to the EOSC thematic node DataTERRA. Three case-study datasets (Quaternary pollen records from Estonia, 7,500-year tree-ring isotope records from the University of Helsinki, and HMS Challenger foraminifera from NHM London) are being used to assess metadata such as object type, taxonomy, origin, age, depositional environment and provenance. A key finding is the mismatch between specimen-level standards (ABCD-EFG, Darwin Core) and DataTERRA's dataset-level DCAT, so the project is mapping between them and will deliver a demonstrator, guidance and an online training workshop on 28-29 October.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Linking specimen-rich GeoCASe records to dataset-level DCAT descriptions could let deep-time collection data feed modern environmental observation infrastructures.
content_items.why_it_matters: Earth science collections hold deep-time environmental records that are largely invisible outside the collections community; connecting them to EOSC could support climate and environmental research.
key_points: Earth science collections allow interdisciplinary, deep-time research but have low visibility, inadequate metadata and limited access.
GeoDARA is funded as a six-month small project under EOSC Gravity and aims to connect GeoCASe to DataTERRA, an EOSC thematic node for environmental and observation data.
Case studies: Estonian pollen records, Finno-Scandinavian tree-ring records (University of Helsinki) with oxygen/carbon isotopes, and HMS Challenger foraminifera (NHM London).
Collections use ABCD-EFG or Darwin Core at specimen level, whereas DataTERRA uses DCAT at dataset level, which cannot carry individual specimen information.
Next steps: complete the metadata assessment, improve datasets and possibly the GeoCASe data model, publish via GeoCASe, map to DCAT and produce a demonstrator plus guidance.
An online training/demonstrator workshop is planned for 28-29 October.

content_items.title: Improving geospecimen provenance and findability in the National Museums Scotland Scottish mineral collection

programme.title: Improving geospecimen provenance and findability in the National Museums Scotland Scottish mineral collection
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract: Geospecimen metadata is only as valuable as it is findable. Specimens can be located through a variety of properties - for example by species, donor, location in the museum or provenance in the field. Unfortunately, place names are not always unique and historic descriptions are often ambiguous, inconsistent, and difficult to georeference at scale. Therefore, grid references are better but how many curators have time to look this up manually? We present a curatorial workflow using the National Museums Scotland collection of Scottish minerals - about 18000 specimens collected over 200 years, with variable quality and certainty of provenance. It reconciles legacy mineral names, standardises locality information, and where possible, links specimens to structured localities and coordinates from external resources such as Mindat API. Provenance is treated not as a single point on a map, but as a spectrum of certainty and scale, ranging from a specific named mine shaft to a whole district or county. Museum documentation can therefore preserve uncertainty and locality granularity that are often flattened in external resources. Linking collection records with Mindat can strengthen locality data through grid references and occurrence context, while the museum record retains curatorial detail. This process improves discovery by enabling specimens to be found by searching at any scale, from broad region to specific locality. Museums can not only draw on external data but also use internal collection records to identify missing or faulty data. Moreover, minerals in the collection not yet recorded from Scotland in Mindat are readily identified. This enriches both information sources, and demonstrates geocollections as active contributors to data infrastructure development.

speakers.name: Sarah Stewart
speakers.affiliation: University of Edinburgh (PhD student; internship at National Museums Scotland)

content_items.summary: Sarah Stewart, a computational chemistry PhD student, reported on a two-month internship improving provenance for the roughly 18,000-specimen Scottish mineral collection at National Museums Scotland. She merged transcribed historical ledgers with modern museum records, parsed locality strings into hierarchical levels, standardised names to IMA species and Dana/Strunz classes, and matched unique localities to Mindat to add coordinates, using Python scripts plus manual review. The pipeline exposed record problems (26,000 records for 18,000 specimens, about 1,000 without IDs, 15,000 duplicates needing triage) and resulted in 16,000 validated specimens, while the museum contributed new species occurrences and almost 2,000 new localities back to Mindat.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A scripted, reviewable workflow can quickly reconcile legacy mineral records and enrich them with Mindat coordinates, while giving data back to the community resource.
content_items.why_it_matters: Shows a transferable, low-cost approach for georeferencing and cleaning geological collection data, and a two-way model of exchange with crowdsourced databases like Mindat.
key_points: The collection spans about 200 years; locality precision ranges from mine depth to just 'Scotland'.
A dual legacy problem: historical ledgers (transcribed) and modern digitised records each contain information missing from the other.
Localities were split into hierarchical levels (country, county, region/loch, town/parish/hill, quarry/mine) to preserve detail that external databases often flatten.
Mindat localities were evaluated for feature type and how coordinates should be treated (e.g. mine entrance vs mountain summit).
Scripts took about a day to run/write; the whole project took two months.

Gave to Mindat: about 900 new species occurrences, 475 existing localities and almost 2,000 new localities; gained just over 5,000 Scottish specimens' worth of locality information and mineral coverage data.
Coverage analysis found 366 minerals recorded from Scotland not held in the collection, and 11 held by the museum not otherwise known from Scotland.
Scripts are openly available on GitHub; the workflow is transferable to other collections.
datasets: National Museums Scotland Scottish mineral collection records
methods: Fuzzy matching with Gaelic-English name translation

notable_claims.claim: Systematic processing found 26,000 records for about 18,000 specimens, around 1,000 without IDs and 15,000 duplicates needing triage, yielding 16,000 validated specimens.
The museum contributed about 900 new species occurrences, 475 existing and almost 2,000 new localities to Mindat.
Processing Mindat data added coordinates to 52 localities and corrected 33, so external data should not be taken at face value.
366 minerals reported from Scotland are not in the collection, while 11 minerals in the collection are not otherwise known from Scotland.

recommendations: Automate the easy wins but keep a curator in the loop for ambiguous cases such as duplicate place names.

q_and_a.answer_summary: She did not hit that issue; Mindat localities were evaluated, the county-level hierarchy disambiguated same-named places, only full matches were accepted automatically and partial matches were listed for human checking.

content_items.title: Bridging domains: how SESAR supports Earth and biodiversity digital extended specimens

programme.title: Bridging Domains: How SESAR Supports Earth and Biodiversity Digital Extended Specimens
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract:
SESAR, the System for Earth and Extraterrestrial Sample Registration has served as a repository of Earth science specimen metadata since 2004. Scientists and collection managers “register” their specimen with SESAR, and SESAR provides them with a stable landing page containing metadata describing their sample, and a persistent identifier (an IGSN, or International Generic Sample Number, now managed by DataCite). Though originally focused in the Earth and geological science community, SESAR has gradually expanded to additional domains such as archaeology, paleontology, and environmental sciences. SESAR currently supports 1000+ individual researchers and dozens of collections, globally, in making their sample records publicly accessible, providing an open, global catalog and discovery platform for researchers to find samples and specimens. In this presentation, we provide an overview of SESAR and present the outcomes of a five-year database migration and modernization project, focusing on the ways in which we have integrated and formalized our adoption of broader community vocabularies and standards, such as GeoSciML, and our ongoing efforts to support Darwin Core. We share ways the new database enables greater flexibility in incorporating new community vocabularies and in better supporting the unique needs of organizations and curated collections. We conclude by sharing how SESAR supports the community vision of a “digital extended specimen.”

Corresponding author

Natalie Raia University of Arizona, College of Information Science

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded virtual talk; SESAR is transcribed as 'SESR'/'CSAR' and PI Kerstin Lehnert as 'Kirsten Leonard'. The host added a note afterwards (01:14:07) that the speaker runs an ESIP physical samples group.

content_items.summary: Andrea Thomer introduced SESAR (System for Earth and Extraterrestrial Sample Registration), a nearly 20-year-old registry at Columbia University that mints IGSNs (now DataCite DOIs) for physical samples and holds over five million samples from more than 1,800 users, including a growing number of biodiversity records. She previewed a major migration under way that week: a redesigned search portal, sample landing pages with maps and sample 'family' links, an improved Workbench, and adoption of an application profile of the iSamples Earth and environmental material vocabulary (thousands rather than hundreds of terms). SESAR supports digital extended specimens by storing IGSNs, other identifiers and semantically rich links to related resources that propagate to DataCite Commons, and is developing a Darwin Core crosswalk and profiles for other communities.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Persistent sample identifiers plus linked metadata propagated to DataCite let samples be connected to their derived research products across Earth and biodiversity domains.
content_items.why_it_matters: Shows how a mature geoscience PID infrastructure can support biodiversity collections and the digital extended specimen vision.
key_points: SESAR was founded in 2004 by Kerstin Lehnert and fully operational since 2009; it is the birthplace of the IGSN.
IGSN (International Generic Sample Number) is now effectively a DOI managed by DataCite, giving unambiguous links from papers and datasets to samples.
The new system has a redesigned search portal, landing pages with maps and links to parent/sibling samples, and an improved Workbench with registration, usage metrics and team permissions.
SESAR metadata stores the IGSN, local catalogue/field numbers and explicit semantic links to related digital resources, which are propagated to DataCite Commons for network traversal and metrics.
Adopts a lightly edited application profile of the iSamples Earth and environmental science material vocabulary (by Steve Richard).
The new architecture eases extension vocabularies; a SESAR-to-Darwin Core crosswalk and Darwin Core sample profile are in development, with Illinois Natural History Survey herpetology as a test case.
Planned profiles for marine/lacustrine core repositories, astromaterials/meteorites and tephra.
NSF and IMLS grants support hackathons, webinars, tutorials and roadmaps for sample metadata sharing.

Related-resource links in SESAR metadata are propagated to DataCite, allowing the network of samples and outputs to be traversed in DataCite Commons.
The new material vocabulary uses a couple of thousand terms instead of a couple of hundred.

content_items.title: Developing and implementing a relational mineral taxonomy model in EMu for Museums Victoria's mineral collection

programme.title: [Skipped talk] Developing and implementing relational mineral taxonomy model in EMu for Museums Victoria's Mineral Collection
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract:
Mineral identification and classification data in Museum’s Victoria’s (MV's) EMu CMS have until recently been stored within individual specimens’ catalogue records and managed as part of a series of shared hierarchical look-up-lists. This is unlike MV's biological taxonomic data, which have made use of a one-to-many relational structure between taxonomy and catalogue records at least since the implementation of EMu in the late 1990’s. Disadvantages of the model previously applied to mineral data include difficulties making changes following nomenclature revisions, an inability to capture incomplete taxonomy (eg. cataloguing specimens only identified to the level of a group or solid solution series), and a limited ability to query the database on mineral properties, chemistry or classification schemes.

I report on the development and implementation of a relational mineral taxonomy model in EMu over 2025-26. This model captures a hierarchy of mineral taxonomy; subgroup, group and supergroup as formlised by the International Mineralogical Association (IMA) in 2009, the Dana and Strunz classification systems, ideal chemical formula and elements, and IMA approval status. It also allows use of some existing functionality for zoological taxonomy, capturing the history of identification and linking taxonomy records to publications in which species were described or revised. Data to populate 6,125 taxonomy records for IMA approved mineral species were extracted from Mindat.org via their API. A further 162 taxonomy records for invalid, as yet undescribed, or incompletely classified specimens were created and manually populated. These 6,287 taxonomy records have been linked to the 56,792 catalogue records containing mineral identification data in MV's database.

speakers.name: Oskar Lindenmayer
speakers.affiliation: Museums Victoria (Collection Manager, Geosciences)

actual.identification_notes: The programme marks this talk as skipped, but its pre-recording was played in full after Andrea Thomer's talk. Name transcribed as 'Oscar Lindenmeyer'.

content_items.summary: Oskar Lindenmayer described moving Museums Victoria's 57,000-specimen mineral collection (about 2,500 species, 131 type specimens) from classification stored locally in each EMu catalogue record to shared mineral taxonomy records in EMu's taxonomy module. The model adopts IMA hierarchy terms (species, subgroup, group, supergroup, plus other rank/value), keeps Dana class/code for legacy while adding Strunz-Mindat classes, handles solid-solution series such as wolframite via a multi-valued series field outside the hierarchy, and separates ideal formula and ideal elements. Catalogue records were linked to shell taxonomy records holding Mindat IDs before the new fields existed, then populated rapidly via the OpenMindat API, with about 150 non-standard records created manually.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Linking catalogue records to shared, Mindat-populated mineral taxonomy records makes mineral identification data consistent and queryable.
content_items.why_it_matters: Gives mineral collections a template for relational, standards-aligned classification data in a common CMS, reusing infrastructure built for biological taxonomy.
key_points: Previously group and class were stored per catalogue record, producing inconsistencies across records for the same species.
New taxonomy records (e.g. vanadinite) are shared by all catalogue records; some fields are mirrored back to the catalogue for querying.
IMA 2009 hierarchy terms are used; other rank/value handles non-standard cases and the amphibole supergroup's fourth level.
Dana classification has not been updated since 1997, so Strunz-Mindat class/code are recorded alongside it.
A multi-valued series field lets a search for 'wolframite' return ferberite, hübnerite and series-level records without the whole wolframite group; series can span groups.
EMu cannot render subscripts/superscripts, so a plain-text human-readable formula convention was adopted.
Legacy data were copied into a locked field first; shell records with EMu IRN, Mindat ID and name allowed linking before implementation.
IMA status and status date capture discredited names without overwriting historical identifications; varieties remain in the catalogue record.
methods: Bulk population via API using a shared identifier

notable_claims.claim: The collection has about 57,000 mineral specimens representing about 2,500 species, including 131 type specimens, around half of type minerals lodged in Australian institutions.

content_items.title: Understanding geological specimen use for effective digitisation strategies

programme.title: Understanding Geological Specimen Use for Effective Digitisation Strategies
programme.session: SYM06 Rocks, Minerals, and Metadata: Integrating Earth Sciences into the TDWG Community
programme.abstract:
Without representation on major international platforms like GBIF, geological collections are currently much less digitally accessible to user communities than digitised biological specimens. Improving the access of users requires the digitisation of more geological and mineralogical specimens and the appropriate representation of their associated data. Forthcoming standards like the TDWG Mineralogy Extension and Minimum Information for a Digital Specimen (MIDS) will provide a framework with new fields that will enable the sharing of expressive top-level data, but there is a clear need for a better understanding what the audiences for these collections need from this data as we plan how to digitize and share collections data.

Here we present the preliminary longitudinal study of the users and use cases of geological and mineralogy specimens in museums, especially in three long-established well-known collections - the Smithsonian Institution, Natural History Museum of London, and National Museums Scotland. We analyze use of our specimens recorded in the published literature (including journals), loan forms, audience demographics, and web search. These data enable us to better understand the granularity of kind of data our audiences need and to develop more effective strategies about what and how to digitise.

programme.abstract: In 1996, the Catalogue of Life (CoL) was planned as a comprehensive inventory of all valid species known to biological science globally. Creating this list required a coherent classification and representative synonymy. The first edition of CoL was published on CD in 2001.The Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS) became a major data provider, contributing over half of the species in the first edition (incl. mammals, birds, and many other groups). Crucially, ITIS also provided the global hierarchy that served as the CoL Management Classification for many years. The Species Files, another big US contributor, joined CoL in 2004, gradually adding global checklists for Orthoptera, Blattodea, Phasmida, Aphidomorpha, Mantodea, Plecoptera, Embioptera, Coreoidea, Psocodea, Dermaptera, Lygaeoidea, Isoptera, etc. Over 25 CoL annual editions, other US-based global databases have participated in CoL: Hexorallians of the world (2002-2017); ICTV (2002-); Moss TROPICOS (2002-2022); Systema Dipterorum (2005-); LecyPages (2007-2017); LDL Neuropterida (2009-); Brassicaceae (2010-2023); Early Land Plants Today (2010-2022); 3i Auchenorrhyncha (2011-); Membracoidea of the World Database (2011-2024); Entiminae (2016-); PBI Plant Bug (2016-); The World List of Cycads (2016-); PaleoBioDB (2017-); Gymnodinium (2018-); Jewel Beetles (2018-); StaphBase (2019-); Sepidiini tribe (2021-); World Catalogue of Opiliones (2021-); Global Lepidoptera Index (2022-); Bryonames (2023-); LWS fleas (2023-); The World Odonata List (2023-); AntCat (2025-). By 2025, US-based and expert-curated databases contributed 793,339 species, or 36% of the entire 2.2-million-species CoL base release. content_items.title: A knowledge organisation system for taxonomic data

programme.title: A Knowledge Organisation System for Taxonomic Data
programme.session: CO1 National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
programme.abstract:
With the Taxon Concept Standard (TCS) now ratified, the community has a framework to better organize taxonomic data. While often designed for specific Floras, these models can serve as reference implementations for TCS and broader Knowledge Organisation Systems (KOS). This presentation introduces a model developed for VicFlora that is oriented around the Taxon Concept as the core of the system, with all other data layers acting as supporting components.

The model is structured across six key layers:

Semantics: Taxon Concepts and mappings Syntax: Names, relations, usages, and typification Governance: Taxon trees and versioned nodes Authority: Provenance (references) and attribution (agents) Narrative: Profiles and descriptions Identity: External identifiers.

To manage complexity, we employ a "sidecar" pattern. Extension sidecars manage name types and reference roles, while functional sidecars allow Taxon Concepts to remain immutable, while their context can change. By decoupling these, we can update classifications (via Tree Nodes) or modify descriptive content (via Profiles) without redefining the concept itself. The Profile serves as the primary extension point, bridging internal models with other TDWWG standards like Plinian Core, Darwin Core, and SDD.

We distinguish between narrowly defined relationships and polymorphic ones-such as provenance and attribution-which require flexible handling. This architecture provides a blueprint for building taxonomic systems that are theoretically sound under TCS and functionally agile, demonstrating how a concept-centric KOS can effectively integrate keys, maps, and occurrences.

content_items.summary: Niels Klazenga argued that problems with taxonomic checklists are data-quality issues that are fixable, and presented a layered data model developed as a reference implementation for his flora following ratification of TCS 2 (Taxon Concept Schema) last December. The model separates concerns into semantics (taxon concepts), syntax (names, typification, usages), authority (references, agents), governance (taxon trees and revisions) and narrative (profiles), plus identity, infrastructure and extension layers, using 'sidecar' patterns to keep taxon concepts immutable. He mapped layers to TCS, Plinian Core and Darwin Core, noted that governance is not covered by any standard, and proposed a conceptual model for taxon data developed with the Darwin Core maintenance group.

content_items.title: Managing observations when taxonomy changes: the case of Artportalen and Dyntaxa

programme.title: Managing observations when taxonomy changes: the case of Artportalen and Dyntaxa
programme.session: CO1 National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
programme.abstract:
In the Swedish taxonomic database Dyntaxa (www.dyntaxa.se), updates are published continuously. This taxonomy is used by the Swedish citizen observatory Artportalen (www.artportalen.se). However, while about one million observations are added to Artportalen every two months, updates of taxonomy are only made once during this time.

In Dyntaxa, the taxon, with its corresponding taxonID, is the basis. The name for such a taxon can change without changing taxonID. Lumps are easy to deal with by pointing an unaccepted taxon (with its taxonID) to the accepted one. Technically, splits can also be dealt with automatically by keeping all observations on the old (sensu lato) taxon, even though it is no longer considered a species but essentially a collective taxon. However, this is usually unsatisfactory. When there is more information about the split you might be able to move observations to one or several of the new species. In Sweden, these cases are relatively few despite the volume of observations.

Another way is to inform the reporter of such observations of these changes. They will be presented with the option to move them if they now know what new species they observed.

The Dyntaxa data model can handle not only these relations between taxa, such as splits and different kinds of lumps, but also convey the reason for them and the statuses of the taxa involved. When an editor is working in Dyntaxa, lumping a species with another, an automated text is generated. This text summarizes which taxonIDs were involved and that, e.g., taxonID 25 was merged into taxonID 42. This is also stored in a machine-readable format in the database.

We show examples where automation works fine, and some where we currently assess them manually but could possibly automate more in the future.

content_items.summary: Johan Liljeblad explained how Sweden's 26-year-old citizen observatory Artportalen stays aligned with the national taxonomic database (Dyntaxa, started 2004), which uses stable taxon-concept identifiers rather than names. Taxonomy is published continuously and harvested nightly, but Artportalen applies changes every two months with news notes: name changes need no action, lumps move observations to the new taxon ID, and splits keep observations on a 'collective taxon' unless information (e.g. geography or phenology) allows assignment to one segregate. Edge cases include chained lumps, excluded taxa and fully revised concepts, so the process remains semi-manual with expert review, which is manageable at about 100 new taxa and 10-15 reassignments per cycle.

content_items.title: Modernizing Brazil's taxonomic backbone: how ChecklistBank supports biodiversity and genetic heritage systems

programme.title: Modernizing Brazil’s Taxonomic Backbone: How ChecklistBank Supports Biodiversity and Genetic Heritage Systems
programme.session: CO1 National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
programme.abstract:
Brazil, has made major advances in organizing and managing taxonomic information. It is one of the few countries with two official and continuously maintained national species catalogues: one for Flora and Funga and another for Fauna, curated by more than 800 taxonomists.

Both lists are published monthly using IPT and shared with GBIF and ChecklistBank. Taxonomy is the essential backbone for biodiversity information systems, since taxonomic updates require continuous reprocessing of species occurrence records.

Brazil operates two major systems dependent on an updated taxonomic backbone: SiBBr - Brazilian Biodiversity Information System), a Living Atlases platform and SISGEN, the Brazilian Genetic Heritage Management System, where all research involving genetic heritage must legally register activities and outputs.

ChecklistBank has played a key role in strengthening Brazil’s biodiversity taxonomic backbone. Initially, it supported detailed quality assessment of the official lists, identifying duplicated names, typographical errors, inconsistencies in Portuguese Darwin Core terminology, and other standardization issues. More recently, it enabled the construction of a unified Brazilian taxonomic backbone by integrating the two official catalogues, incorporating invasive species, generating identifiers for taxonomic tree construction, merging extensions, and producing a Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A) directly consumed by national systems.

Previously, this workflow in SiBBr required extensive technical effort to clean, harmonize, and generate updated taxonomic files. With ChecklistBank and the support of its technical team, the process became more efficient, transforming a complex operation into a routine update performed every six months.

content_items.title: Building a taxonomic reference authority for conservation: the Digital Catalogue of Biodiversity of Poland

programme.title: Building a Taxonomic Reference Authority for Conservation: The Digital Catalogue of Biodiversity of Poland
programme.session: CO1 National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
programme.abstract:
The Digital Catalogue of Biodiversity of Poland (DCBP) is a comprehensive inventory of all confirmed eukaryotic species and Cyanobacteria within Poland's administrative borders. The content is divided into taxonomic chapters managed by expert authors responsible for validating species composition and taxon attributes. These attributes cover occurrence status, threat categories, invasiveness, and other expandable characteristics. Each species entry is backed by a published reference or expert opinion documenting its presence in the country.

Currently, the DCBP comprises 100+ chapters published as individual GBIF checklist datasets and integrated into the Biodiversity Map (BioMap) portal, developed by the Polish GBIF Node. The total repository contains 73K species, including 36.7K animals, 19.9K fungi, 9.9K plants, 4.9K chromists, 0.5K protozoans, and 0.9K bacteria.

DCBP taxa belong to the taxonomic tree of the BioMap database, built on a PostgreSQL relational framework. This architecture connects checklists, species occurrences, datasets, collections, publications, and authors. The BioMap portal enables authors to manage their respective lists, edit or add new taxa, and update literature sources. Furthermore, the DCBP maps Catalogue of Life (CoL) taxon identifiers to facilitate external interoperability. We aim to establish the DCBP as the primary reference authority supporting Polish biodiversity research and conservation. Alongside other European national checklists, the Catalogue may serve as a valuable foundation for regional initiatives.

It covers all eukaryotes and cyanobacteria recorded for Poland (over 65,000 species in 107 chapters), each backed by at least one reference and a presence status, using an ITIS-based taxonomy model with role-based permissions. Each chapter is published to GBIF and synchronised to ChecklistBank; a portal offers interactive summaries and graphical views, and plans include DNA barcodes, printed publications and a Europe-wide network of comparable national checklists.

programme.title: National Biodiversity Information Action Campaign Production Process: A Case Study of Taiwan
programme.session: CO1 National & Global Taxonomic Backbones
programme.abstract:
With the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (K-MGBF), a robust biodiversity information infrastructure is essential for Taiwan’s conservation goals. Since 2021, the Taiwan Biodiversity Information Alliance (TBIA) has implemented a national biodiversity data integration initiative through the 2021-2025 Action Campaign, focusing on species occurrence data, a Biodiversity Database Portal, inter-agency collaboration, and data standardization.

Building on this foundation, the 2026-2030 Campaign shifts toward long-term system resilience and operational sustainability. The Campaign was co-developed by an inter-agency working group, drawing on five years of experience while highlighting challenges in cross-domain coordination and staffing capacity.

Despite progress, key challenges remain in cross-domain governance, data circulation, integration of long-term monitoring needs such as Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs), and sustainable institutional and financial support.

In response, the Campaign defines five strategic directions: enhancing data openness and quality; strengthening interoperability via APIs and taxonomic checklists; building a comprehensive public-private network with stable funding; facilitating inter-agency technical exchange; and enhancing data usability through improved validation and citation practices. These strategies address governance, technical, data, and financial dimensions of infrastructure resilience.

This framework serves as an implementation-oriented synthesis, translating strategy into actionable guidance. This case study illustrates how biodiversity data infrastructures can evolve toward greater resilience, offering a reference for similar global initiatives.

content_items.title: Metadata matters: perceptions on the implementation of Darwin Core in the biocollections cyberinfrastructure

programme.title: Metadata Matters: Perceptions on the Implementation of Darwin Core and Other Considerations in the Biocollections Cyberinfrastructure
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract: Bio-and geo-collections inform scientific discovery, advance knowledge, influence policy decisions, and serve as educational resources. Aggregating biocollections data requires several steps from curation of physical items, data capture and digitization, and creating DarwinCore (DwC) compliant metadata to allow for discoverability in institutional, discipline-specific, and data repositories such as GBIF. With differing curation practices over time, technological and methodological advancements, and evolving funding priorities, the physical research objects, their associated metadata, and derived data and media create a complicated cyberinfrastructure. This survey of curators and collection managers was conducted to better understand their perspectives on the data curation of biocollections. The survey focused on the characteristics of collections professionals, their data storage, access, and reuse practices, challenges to DwC metadata implementation, and who their anticipated users are. Recruitment through TDWG, iDigBio, SPNHC, and discipline-specific listservs led to 60 usable responses. Half of respondents held doctoral degrees, had been in their roles for more than 10 years, and 75% worked at academic institutions. Many themes emerged in relation to perceived roadblocks when mapping to data standards, such as data complexity and representing linked or derived data, gaps in standards development and community implementation guidelines as well as discipline-specific data practices, capacity and technical challenges, and a need for continued support and education around implementing standards and communicating changes or new terminology. The results can inform the building of a robot-ready cyberinfrastructure to increase data access and reuse.

content_items.summary: Wade Bishop, a social scientist, presented results of a survey (57 responses, about 98% from the US) of collections staff on Darwin Core implementation, building on earlier interviews and focus groups. Respondents were mostly senior collection managers or curators in academic settings who largely learned data skills on the job; 82% deposit data in GBIF. content_items.title: Pinned insect digitization conveyor: image and data transcription workflows

programme.title: Pinned Insect Digitization Conveyor: image and data transcription workflows
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract: The Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History (NMNH) is currently digitizing pollinating insects using a Pinned Insect Digitization Conveyor developed by Picturae. The digital workflow, developed by the Smithsonian Office of Digital and Innovation, the NMNH Informatics and Data Science Center, and the Department of Entomology, are reviewed here. Insects and labels are placed on the conveyor and up to 1,500 specimens are processed daily. Four images are captured of each insect - one of labels and three focus-stacked images of the specimen. Conveyor images are run through a technical review process and are screened by Picturae before delivery to Smithsonian. Files are organized into a folder system which hold all specimen images from an insect drawer. A second technical check, using the Smithsonian system, Osprey, is followed by review of random images by an individual. Imaging errors may include issues related to automated focus stacking and specimens being captured at the wrong resolution for their size. When a drawer has passed QC, images are delivered to the institutional DAMS. A script then picks up the images for inclusion into the NMNH database of record, EMu. Stub records are created, images are attached, and the record is then published. Label images are submitted to a different vendor for data transcription. Transcribed data are run through Osprey where a review of randomly selected data is checked for accuracy. When a drawer has passed QC, data is transformed for bulk import back into EMu. Data is appended to the original stub records and images are made available for Open Access (CC0), if applicable. The current project goal is the digitization of 365,000 specimens of pinned insects of which the majority are pollinating insects.

content_items.title: X-raying wild plant seeds: preparing images for future AI-driven global biodiversity research

programme.title: X-raying wild plant seeds: Preparing images for future AI-driven global biodiversity research
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract: X-ray imaging is an effective non-destructive method for assessing seed quality in seed banks, enabling the identification of full, empty or damaged seeds when estimating the proportion of potentially viable seeds within a sample. This method is routinely used at the Millennium Seed Bank, RBG, Kew, as an alternative to destructive cut-testing for evaluating seed lot quality. Over the past 25 years, more than 100,000 seed x-ray images have been captured, providing a valuable resource for documenting seed traits in wild plants (e.g., shape, size, length, width, and internal features). Here, we describe the processing of these images to generate a corresponding image with a structured grid overlay and standardised measuring scale, to support future AI-driven research to measure features. The image-processing script is Python-based and uses Pillow for standard image manipulation and pydicom for parsing medical-grade X-ray metadata. Script converts digital pixel data into a calibrated physical reference through a three-step mathematical transformation: (1) metadata extraction identifies image resolution from file headers by reading dots per Inch (DPI); for standard JPEGs, this is obtained via Pillow, while for DICOM files, resolution is derived from pixel spacing or equivalent tags using pydicom; (2) pixel-to-metric conversion computes pixels per centimetre using standard conversions, enabling grid intervals according to image resolution; and (3) grid placement generates an evenly spaced coordinated sequence across image dimensions. Scale accuracy is validated against physical seed length measurements from a representative sample. This workflow standardises legacy and newly acquired x-ray images, enabling downstream computational and AI-driven global biodiversity research.

content_items.summary: Robert Turner explained how Kew is migrating 21 years of Millennium Seed Bank seed X-ray images (used for non-destructive seed quality testing: healthy, empty or infested seeds) from a network drive into its digital asset management system and linking them to collections data. As part of Kew's 2021-2026 digitisation programme and new Integrated Collections Management System (Earthscape, occurrence-centred with links to WCVP/POWO and Index Fungorum), Python tools add a resolution-based grid and scale bar to each image, validated against physical seed measurements. Images go into the Digifolia DAMS, are exposed via S3/CloudFront URLs linked in Earthscape, and will reach users through the Kew data portal and the future Seed Pod portal, subject to checking material and data agreements.

content_items.title: Next-generation digitization: integrating spectral reflectance into the online mobilization of herbaria

programme.title: Next-Generation Digitization: Integrating spectral reflectance into the online mobilization of herbaria
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract: Spectral reflectance is emerging as a prime candidate for next-generation herbarium digitization, as spectra provide non-destructive information on taxonomic identity and functional traits. We have operationalized digitization of spectral reflectance in the Missouri Botanical Garden Herbarium (MO) using a pipeline that runs in parallel to our specimen imaging and transcription workflow. Spectral measurements follow the protocol of the International Herbarium Spectral Digitization (IHerbSpec) working group - ensuring reproducibility and interoperability of spectra across the world’s herbaria - and are linked by keying on specific metadata with their corresponding specimen records in the collection management system, Tropicos. To date, our pipeline has resulted in >60,000 spectral measurements taken on >10,000 herbarium specimens (and counting), focusing on groups in which MO curators have taxonomic expertise. We are using these spectral measurements for research applications ranging from taxonomy to ecology, including, but not limited to, using spectra to detect misidentified specimens, predict ploidy, and evaluate how Amazonian trees have responded to climate change.

speakers.name: Matthew Austin
speakers.affiliation: Missouri Botanical Garden

content_items.summary: Matthew Austin described how Missouri Botanical Garden, with philanthropic support to digitise its roughly eight million herbarium specimens, is adding spectral reflectance as a 'third layer' of digitisation alongside images and transcribed labels. After imaging and barcoding, a spectral team takes three point measurements per leaf surface on selected specimens (leaves liftable onto a black background, free of glue or pathogens, woody taxa with in-house curatorial expertise), recording rich per-scan metadata under the protocol of iHerbSpec, a 30+ institution working group. Data are linked in Tropicos by barcode; about 1.55 million specimens have been imaged and 16,000 have spectra, and clade-specific species identification models trained on expert-identified spectra achieve accuracies around the 90s, even identifying sterile specimens.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Spectral reflectance can be captured at scale during herbarium digitisation and supports accurate species identification from leaves alone.
content_items.why_it_matters: Extends the digital extended specimen with chemistry/phenotype data and shows a standardised cross-institution protocol for making it reusable.
key_points: Spectral reflectance encodes chemical and physical properties and can infer functional traits and aid identification.
The project also funds a curatorial mentorship programme pairing 18 digitisation staff with curators.

iHerbSpec developed the first standardised protocol for herbarium spectral measurements, with file naming and metadata conventions; it meets annually in person and monthly online.

content_items.title: Experience of collaborative management of the World Auchenorrhyncha Database in TaxonWorks

programme.title: Experience of collaborative management of the World Auchenorrhyncha Database in TaxonWorks
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract:
The World Auchenorrhyncha Database (WAD) initially began as a series of smaller projects managed using the 3i software platform (http://dmitriev.speciesfile.org). The 3i system was based on an MS Access database linked to custom web interfaces and was designed to provide detailed information on species taxonomy, nomenclature, distribution, biological associations, bibliography, and identification tools, including interactive and dichotomous keys.

Eight years ago, all Auchenorrhyncha-related projects were merged into a single database, and the data were migrated to TaxonWorks (https://taxonworks.org), an open-source biodiversity information workbench developed to replace three previously available platforms: 3i, mx, and SpeciesFiles. Migrating data from legacy databases into TaxonWorks created numerous opportunities for collaborative data entry and management.

Following the migration, the number of curators and users with extended access rights increased substantially, from only one or a few individuals to more than 65 contributors. In addition to implementing global nomenclatural changes within the group, curators now focus on more applied goals, such as adding species images, developing interactive and dichotomous identification keys, and refining distributional data to produce comprehensive regional species checklists.

Although many users are not directly involved in data editing, they continue to contribute significantly by commenting on nomenclatural and taxonomic issues and by sharing bibliographic resources and photographs. The global coverage of the WAD currently exceeds 48,150 valid species (https://hoppers.speciesfile.org), and its data are shared across major global biodiversity initiatives, including Catalogue of Life, GBIF, iNaturalist, Global Names.

content_items.summary: Dmitry Dmitriev described how the World Auchenorrhyncha Database (leafhoppers, planthoppers, cicadas and relatives) grew from a largely single-person project into a collaborative one after migration to TaxonWorks, now with 66 registered users. He toured the TaxonPages public interface: species pages with synonymy, nomenclatural history, type information, specimen- and country-level distribution maps, downloadable distribution records, host-plant associations, iNaturalist images, interactive and dichotomous keys generated from morphological matrices, and pictorial image matrices built from contributors' 28,000 images. Data flow to the Catalogue of Life and GBIF, and iNaturalist now pulls the classification directly from the TaxonWorks API; feedback arrives through GitHub issues.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: TaxonWorks turned a personal taxonomic database into a collaborative, well-connected resource feeding Catalogue of Life, GBIF and iNaturalist.
content_items.why_it_matters: An example of how a modern taxonomic platform supports collaborative curation, identification tools and downstream data sharing for a large insect group.

content_items.title: Digitising heritage for science: the Medical Entomology Museum as a platform for entomological biodiversity research and vector-borne disease surveillance

programme.title: Digitising heritage for science: The Medical Entomology Museum as a platform for entomological biodiversity research and vector-borne disease surveillance
programme.session: CO2 Digitizing Collections & Legacy Data
programme.abstract: The Medical Entomology Museum (MEM) integrates heritage and science by maintaining one of Africa’s significant collections of arthropods of medical importance. Established primarily to support malaria and vector-borne disease research, the museum houses specimens collected over the past century. These collections serve as an important resource for species identification, biodiversity studies, and monitoring ecological and environmental changes that influence public health. This presentation highlights the museum’s role as both a historical archive and a dynamic research resource supporting FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) biodiversity data standards. Ongoing digitisation efforts aim to convert legacy specimen records, including type material, archival collections, and historically under-curated or orphaned datasets, into structured, machine-readable formats suitable for integration into global biodiversity informatics systems. These outputs support biodiversity research and strengthen vector-borne disease surveillance through improved accessibility, interoperability, and analytical readiness. The digitised collections also provide baseline data for malaria and vector surveillance, enabling historical comparisons and trend analysis. Beyond its scientific contribution, the museum provides insight into the history of medically important insect research in southern Africa and the development of public health interventions. It also promotes public awareness by transforming preserved collections into accessible tools for learning and engagement. In this way, the MEM demonstrates how heritage institutions contribute to science, biodiversity data innovation, and stronger public health systems.

programme.title: How is digitisation doing? Monitoring the increase in digitised collections using MIDS
programme.session: SYM22 State of the Collections Description Interest Group. What's Happening and What's Not!
programme.abstract: The Minimum Information about a Digital Specimen (MIDS) standard has been under development by the TDWG MIDS task group for several years and entered expert review in early 2026. It provides a framework for automatically and reproducibly assessing the digitisation level achieved by a specimen, based on its provided data properties. Applying the MIDS level calculation to historical and recent GBIF specimen data snapshots, we shed light on the growth of digitised specimen collections in recent years and investigate patterns across the dimensions of taxonomy, preservation type, location, and age.

speakers.name: Elspeth Haston
speakers.affiliation: Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh (Deputy Herbarium Curator)

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded talk; Elspeth Haston joined live for Q&A. Moderator's introduction of her institution transcribed as 'RBGQ'.

content_items.summary: Elspeth Haston reported a MIDS-based analysis of ten years (since 2016) of preserved-specimen records of biological taxa in GBIF, using full-GBIF Darwin Core downloads partitioned with DuckDB into Parquet and scored with a version of the MIDS calculator (2017 excluded for data problems). Progress was real but not steady: record numbers reaching MIDS 1 and 2 grew, yet the percentage stayed fairly flat as total records grew, with a big jump in MIDS 1 after 2016 driven by GBIF enforcing licences and more datasets providing modified dates. Newly arriving records vary a lot, some cohorts decline (one institution's datasets dropped organisation data for two years), enhancement tools have uneven impact, kingdoms differ in data completeness, and big datasets have big effects.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: MIDS can monitor global digitisation progress, and GBIF data show completeness improving unevenly and sometimes going backwards.
content_items.why_it_matters: Provides the first longitudinal, standard-based view of how complete published specimen data are and what interventions (e.g. mandatory licences) actually move the needle.
key_points: GBIF snapshots lacked full specimen metadata, so the team used Darwin Core archives from users who downloaded all of GBIF.
Big files need big computing resources; one record had over 60,000 coordinates.
The large MIDS 1 increase after 2016 came from licence enforcement and more modified dates; name and identification are high due to the GBIF backbone.
People identifiers started appearing, showing the effect of dedicated enhancement work, though without raising overall MIDS levels.
Recent years show fewer records arriving below MIDS 0 and more at MIDS 1, driven by organisation and modified fields.
2016 records fell from MIDS 0 to -1 by 2018 because five datasets from one institution dropped organisation data, corrected by 2019.
Animalia more often record object type; Plantae lead on media and media IDs (possibly IIIF); collecting numbers more common in plants and fungi.
methods: Longitudinal MIDS scoring of GBIF records

notable_claims.claim: The percentage of digitised records remained fairly steady over the years because growth in MIDS levels was matched by growth in total records.
Enforcing licence information in GBIF and more datasets including modified dates drove the jump in records reaching MIDS level one.
Records are not just becoming more complete in GBIF; some are decreasing too.

results_findings: Big datasets make a big impact on overall figures.
limitations: 2017 data could not be confidently used and were excluded.
future_work: Further analysis by dataset size and of enhancement over time, requiring additional data in the Parquet files.

q_and_a.question: Did mass digitisation projects producing many lower-quality records affect the numbers?
q_and_a.answer_summary: They began categorising datasets by size; some very large datasets have lower MIDS levels and more analysis and data are needed.

representative_excerpt.text: So the development of the MIDS standard is giving us a way now to measure and monitor global digitization effort to see the impact of all the work being done.

notable_moments.description: Effect of GBIF licence enforcement on MIDS level 1.
Differences between kingdoms in data completeness.

content_items.title: The Latimer Core standard and the Global Registry of Scientific Collections

programme.title: The Latimer Core standard and the Global Registry of Scientific Collections
programme.session: SYM22 State of the Collections Description Interest Group. What's Happening and What's Not!
programme.abstract:
The Global Registry of Scientific Collections (GRSciColl) aims to catalogue physical scientific collections, their content, location, associated staff and institutions. GRSciColl was originally developed before the Latimer Core (LtC) Standard became ratified. It has its own model, terms and associated vocabularies. The information can be stored in different types of entities: Institution and collection entries, which contain a lot of textual descriptions. Specimen occurrence records shared on the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) platform and linked to GRSciColl institution and collection entries. Semi-structured tables called “collection descriptor groups”. They are used to describe collection content and are associated with collection entries. In this presentation, we will show where and how GRSciColl is integrating the LtC standard: GRSciColl entries can be accessed as well as uploaded in the LtC standard. GRSciColl collection descriptors groups use the LtC terms and suggested vocabularies. The objectClassificationName term is particularly useful when capturing information about subcollections corresponding to polyphyletic groups. It allows for example to find collections containing algae: https://scientific-collections.gbif.org/collection/search? objectClassification=Algae The use of LtC standard in training material for modelling of collection data.

We will also highlight some of the challenges of this integration.

speakers.name: Marie Grosjean
speakers.affiliation: GBIF Secretariat (data administrator, GRSciColl)

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded talk (restarted after a false start); Marie Grosjean answered live. GRSciColl transcribed as 'GRcycle'/'GR Cycle'.

content_items.summary: Marie Grosjean explained how GRSciColl, the community-curated registry of scientific collections and institutions maintained by GBIF, uses Latimer Core. Collection descriptors are flat tables that fill the gap between textual collection descriptions and specimen-level occurrences, using Darwin Core (dwc:) or Latimer Core (ltc:) headers; GRSciColl currently indexes Latimer Core biome type and object classification name, enabling searches such as marine algae collections by country. Latimer Core is also used as an import/export format and in editor training, but limitations include GRSciColl fields without Latimer Core equivalents (forced into measurementOrFact) and missing descriptors in exports, which will be revisited as Latimer Core's structure is formalised.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Latimer Core gives GRSciColl a common language and exchange format for describing collections between free text and specimen records.
content_items.why_it_matters: Collection-level description lets undigitised or geological collections become discoverable, and GRSciColl is a key real-world implementation of Latimer Core.
key_points: GRSciColl registers collections, institutions, codes and identifiers, curated by 70+ editors with Index Herbariorum as a main source; it has an API and can be embedded in GBIF hosted portals.
Collection descriptors capture lists of taxa, collectors, statistics etc. and can include unmapped columns that are displayed but not indexed.
Indexing Latimer Core biome type and object classification name allows finding non-monophyletic groupings like algae collections.
Missouri Botanical Garden's page is an example of a complete descriptor based on a survey.
Many GRSciColl fields must be modelled as measurementOrFact, which users cannot reproduce without knowing the types.
Plans to revise the Latimer Core export to include descriptors and follow the latest Latimer Core structure.
A modelling exercise in the editor curriculum, tested at a DiSSCo Flanders workshop, shows Latimer Core's flexibility.
methods: Collection descriptors as flat tables with dwc:/ltc: headers

notable_claims.claim: GRSciColl currently indexes the Latimer Core terms biome type and object classification name.
Many GRSciColl fields have no Latimer Core equivalent and have to be modelled as measurement or fact.

limitations: Collection descriptors are missing from the Latimer Core export.
GRSciColl cannot formally represent collection hierarchies.
future_work: Revise the Latimer Core export to include collection descriptors and comply with the new structure.
GBIF work programme item to explore formal relationships between entities.

q_and_a.question: How is the nesting of collections and sub-collections, modelled by Latimer Core, reflected in GRSciColl?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Latimer Core is more flexible than GRSciColl; the workaround is separate entries referencing each other via 'incorporated collections', which is not inferred; formal relationships are on the GBIF work programme; GitHub issues are welcome.

notable_moments.description: What collection descriptors are.
Limitations of the current Latimer Core implementation.

content_items.title: Once and future Latimer Core: status update and open conversation

programme.title: Once and Future Latimer Core: Status update and open conversation.
programme.session: SYM22 State of the Collections Description Interest Group. What's Happening and What's Not!
programme.abstract:
Latimer Core (LtC) is the TDWG standard intended to support description and exchange of information about collections and their associated organizational, and preservation contexts. Over the past year, the Maintenance Group has focused on improving its conceptual model, refining documentation, and exploring practical serialization and interoperability patterns that help long-term sustainability and implementation across diverse collection-management environments.

This presentation will provide an overview of the current state of LtC, summarize the work undertaken during 2025-2026, and introduce some implementation examples, including draft JSON and RDF/XML exchange formats. Together, these examples aim to illustrate both the flexibility of the LtC conceptual model and the unresolved questions surrounding structure, identifiers, and semantic interoperability.

The presenters will invite discussion of larger questions that extend to other TDWG efforts: How do we make standards understandable and maintainable for people across different domains of expertise? How should TDWG approach controlled vocabularies and governance? How should we model relationships between terms, and structure their identifiers (IRIs)? How do we document dataset creation, generation, or AI-assisted workflows? What happens when our standards depend on concepts borrowed from outside the TDWG ecosystem?

This session embraces the messier reality of standards work: balancing flexibility and structure, interoperability and usability, technical rigor and human comprehension. The goal is to share where LtC stands today, and invite discussion. How can TDWG standards remain useful, maintainable, and adaptable as biodiversity data practices continue to evolve?

speakers.name: Sharon Grant
speakers.affiliation: Field Museum

content_items.summary: Sharon Grant updated the room on the Latimer Core maintenance group, which meets monthly and describes intentionally grouped things ('Latimer Core is to groups as Darwin Core is to individual occurrences'). Users asked for structure to implement it, which required identifiers; the group discovered that term IRIs obtained at ratification were duplicated with different meanings because of its generic 'has identifier' structure, conflicting with TDWG's globally scoped IRIs. After the group asked TDWG whether standards could formally include structure, TDWG agreed, following Darwin Core DP and Camtrap DP, so Latimer Core is building an LTC DP structure layer for public review later in the year (after MIDS), with a conceptual/relationship layer still to come.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Latimer Core is being restructured as a data package with unique term IRIs, enabled by TDWG now accepting standards with formal structure.
content_items.why_it_matters: The change affects how TDWG standards are defined generally and determines whether collection-level data can be implemented in machines like GRSciColl.
key_points: The group moved from task group to maintenance group, meets monthly and has 15 open issues; MCZbase and another system are exploring implementation.
URIs, IRIs and persistence were explained: persistence requires someone to maintain the string and a resolving service, which costs money.
TDWG issues IRIs for vocabularies, documents and terms; Latimer Core found some term IRIs duplicated with different meanings.
TDWG agreed to formalise how standards document structure (grouping and repeating terms, IRIs for statistics as in MIDS).
LTC DP will define how terms hang together; a new ratification round and public review is planned, after MIDS.
A conceptual layer and term relationships remain future work.
The standard is named after Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer and the coelacanth Latimeria, deliberately honouring a woman who managed a collection.
questions: How should the conceptual layer and relationships among Latimer Core terms be defined?

notable_claims.claim: Because of how Latimer Core was defined, some term IRIs were duplicates that did not mean the same thing.
TDWG agreed to allow standards with formal structure, following Darwin Core DP and Camtrap DP.

recommendations: People with use cases should join the monthly maintenance group calls and review LTC DP when it goes to public review.
future_work: Public review of LTC DP before Christmas, after MIDS
Define the conceptual layer and relationships among terms

q_and_a.question: Why is it called Latimer?
q_and_a.answer_summary: After Latimeria, the coelacanth described via Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer; the group also wanted a standard named after a woman who managed a collection.

representative_excerpt.text: So Latimer Core is to groups as Darwin Core is to individual occurrences, at its essence.

notable_moments.description: Discovery of duplicated IRIs.
